tools.name: search_guidelines
tools.description:
Look a rule up in the UMR guidelines (umr4nlp/umr-guidelines, guidelines.md).

keywords: terms to look for, e.g. "aspect", "modal strength", "have-rel-role-92", ":quant",
"reentrancy". Passages with more of the keywords come first, then those whose heading has
them, then those that mention them most.
max_results: how many passages to return (at most 10).

Returns {"sections": [{"heading": the passage's place in the guidelines ("Part 3. ... > Part
3-3-1. Aspect"), "text": the passage (a section, or a part of a long one)}], "found": how
many passages matched}.

tools.name: propbank_lookup
tools.description:
Look up a lemma and every alternate of it in PropBank (at most 20 per call).

language is "en" or "zh". Returns Markdown: per lemma, every roleset with its roles and all
its examples (the sentence, then each argument; traces such as *T*-1 are PropBank's own),
or "not in PropBank". Lemmas over the limit are not looked up: the last line names them
(call again with them). There is no PropBank for another language (Uzbek): nothing.

tools.name: search_annotations
tools.description:
Find how a case is annotated: gold UMR annotations of whole sentences.

language: "zh" (Chinese) or "en" (English).
keywords: words or pieces to look for, matched anywhere in a sentence or its annotation:
words of the text (e.g. "发生", "wanted to"), concepts ("have-org-role-91", "identity-91"),
roles (":ARG1-of", ":manner"), attribute values (":aspect state"). Sentences with more of the
keywords come first.
max_results: how many gold sentences to return (at most 10).

Returns {"gold": [{"doc", "sentence_number", "sentence", "annotation"}], where annotation is
the sentence's whole annotation (words, sentence-level graph, alignment, document-level
annotation); "found": how many gold sentences matched in all}.

content.content:
## say

### say-01 (say)

- ARG0: Sayer
- ARG1: Utterance
- ARG2: Hearer
- ARG3: Attributive

Example 1 (Transitive): A Lorillard spokeswoman said "This is an old story."
- ARG0: A Lorillard spokeswoman
- ARG1: "This is an old story"
- rel: said

Example 2 (Fronted): [Kent cigarettes were sold]-1, the company said *trace*-1
- ARG0: the company
- ARG1: *trace*-1
- rel: said

Example 3 (Inverted): [What matters is what advertisers will pay]-1, said *trace*-1 Newsweek's chairman
- ARG1: *trace*-1
- ARG0: Newsweek's chairman
- rel: said

Example 4 (Split): S-["What you have to understand," said John [*?*], "is that Philly literally stinks."]
- ARGM-DSP: [*?*] (tag the leaf node of the *?* itself, and '*' link to the S node containing the ENTIRE utterance
- ARG1: [*?*] (tag the parent node)
- ARG0: John
- rel: said

Example 5 (with listener): John said to Mary: "you're an idiot."
- ARG0: John
- ARG2: to Mary
- ARG1: "you're an idiot"
- rel: said

Example 6 (Weird, attributive usage:): "Well that's odd," said John of the disappearance of his nose.
- ARG1: "Well that's odd"
- ARG0: John
- ARG3: of the disappearance of his nose
- rel: said

Example 7 (split utterance): John-1 is said *trace*-1 to be an idiot.
- ARG1: *trace*-1 to be an idiot
- rel: said

### say-02 (discourse function)

- (no roles)

Example 1 (TAKES NO ARGS): Do you think 0 this war is going *-1 to end up...much less popular say a year from now...?
- rel: say

## suffer

### suffer-01 (suffer, endure/undergo something painful)

- ARG0: entity suffering
- ARG1: malady

Example 1 (intransitive): The company's return on equity could suffer if it made a higher bid.
- ARG0: The company's return on equity
- ARGM-MOD: could
- ARGM-ADV: if it made a higher bid
- rel: suffer

Example 2 (with PP-malady): John suffers from delusions of grandeur.
- ARG0: John
- ARG1: from delusions of grandeur
- rel: suffers

Example 3 (with S-malady): Thou shalt not suffer a fool to live.
- ARG0: Thou
- ARGM-MOD: shalt
- ARGM-NEG: not
- ARG1: a fool to live
- rel: suffer

## high

### high-02 (in the upper ranges (altitude, pitch, etc))

- ARG1: entity in the upper ranges
- ARG2: the upper ranges of what (domain)

Example 1 (arg1): This manifests into the devastation we often see in neighborhoods , where-1 the poverty rate is high [*-1].
- ARG1: the poverty rate
- ARGM-LOC: [*-1]
- rel: high

Example 2 (wide range of arg2s): Orchid Beach penthouse is high in altitude, price and glamour
- ARG1: Orchid Beach penthouse
- ARG2: in altitude, price and glamour
- rel: high

Example 3 (argMs, lexicalized comparative alias): The reason specific ethnic groups are targeted for trying to reduce crime is because , for whatever reason , crime overall is often higher statistically in these groups .
- ARGM-CAU: for whatever reason
- ARG1: crime overall
- ARGM-TMP: often
- ARGM-ADV: statistically
- ARGM-LOC: in these groups
- rel: higher

### high-03 (elated, in good spirits)

- ARG0: cause of elation
- ARG1: elated entity

Example 1 (That's a little harsh, but both args.): Still *PRO* Feeling high from that Toy Story 3 trailer? Well, get ready to be disapointed.
- ARGM-TMP: Still
- ARG1: *PRO*
- ARG0: from that Toy Story 3 trailer
- rel: high

### high-04 (stoned, intoxicated)

- ARG0: intoxicant
- ARG1: stoner

Example 1 (both args): Man runs into Ross Campground Church, announces he's high on "bath salts"
- ARG1: he's
- ARG0: on "bath salts"
- rel: high

## pressure

### pressure-01 (apply pressure, pressure someone to do something)

- ARG0: presser
- ARG1: pressed (on)
- ARG2: goal, pressed-for

Example 1 (with goal): Big Board stock specialists, began to have them pressure the exchange to ban program trading.
- ARG0: them
- ARG1: the exchange
- ARG2: to ban program trading
- rel: pressure

Example 2 (without goal): Generally in the quarter, overproduction of gasoline and higher crude oil prices pressured profitability.
- ARGM-DIS: Generally
- ARGM-TMP: in the quarter
- ARG0: overproduction of gasoline and higher crude oil prices
- ARG1: profitability
- rel: pressured

### pressure-02 (move, cause motion by pressure)

- ARG0: mover
- ARG1: moved
- ARGM: ahead, usually

Example 1 (somewhat odd usage): [The Nikkei index]-1 was pressured *trace*-1 down by profit-taking triggered by sharp advances made through this week and fell 151.20 points to 35527.29.
- ARG1: *trace*
- ARGM-DIR: down
- ARG0: by profit-taking triggered by sharp advances made through this week
- rel: pressured

State (3/4)", "text": "There is a type of event, called “inactive actions” by Croft (2012), which is semantically intermediate between states and processes. In many languages, they can be construed either way. For example, English *lie* can occur in the Progressive (*Bill **is lying** on the bed*) or the Simple Present (*The Sandias **lie** to the east of Albuquerque*). And across languages there is variation as to the default construal of inactive actions. The most frequent inactive actions are posture verbs (*sit, stand, lie, hang*), perception verbs (*see/look at, watch, hear/listen to, feel*), some sensation verbs (*ache*), mental activity verbs (*think, understand*), and verbs of operation/function (*work* in *This washing machine **works/is working***). For the UMR annotation, inactive actions in all constructions are annotated as ```state```. If it is unclear whether an event refers to a ```state``` or an ```atelic process```, then the ```imperfective``` annotation value is used. Unlike ```point state``` and ```semelfactive```, achievements don’t revert back to the base state, which is why they’re considered a finer-grained type of ```performance```. The ```directed achievement``` annotation can be further specified based on whether the change is reversible or irreversible. In (3a), the change that the door undergoes can be reversed in that the door can be closed; therefore this is annotated as ```reversible directed achievement```. In (3b), the change that the window undergoes cannot be reversed; therefore this is annotated as ```irreversible directed achievement```. Accomplishments are durative events that can be categorized based on whether the change occurs incrementally or nonincrementally; this is similar to the difference between directed and undirected activities and endeavors. With ```incremental accomplishment```, the change occurs incrementally along the qualitative dimension; in (3c), the pancake is eaten piece-by-piece and each subsequent bite brings the event closer to completion. With ```nonincremental accomplishment```, the change ends up at a distinct result state (as with all types of Performances), but it may not get there in a linear/incremental fashion.
